q: What is a user story?
options: A complete technical specification
A report of what users did last month
A brief description of an outcome for a specific user, and a promise for a conversation to clarify details
A test script
explanation: A user story is a brief description of an outcome from a specific stakeholder's perspective, and is a promise for a conversation to clarify the details.

q: Which is the usual format of a user story?
options: As a (role), I want (goal), so that (benefit)
The system shall (function) within (time limit)
Given (budget), deliver (scope) by (date)
If (risk), then (response)
explanation: A typical user story describes the role (who benefits), the goal (what they need to accomplish) and the motivation or benefit.

q: In the three Cs of a user story, what does "confirmation" refer to?
options: The sponsor's signature
The index card the story is written on
The discussion between the team and the product owner
The acceptance criteria that show the story is done
explanation: Card is the short written story, conversation is the discussion that fills in details, and confirmation is the acceptance criteria used to verify it.
ref: PMI standard teaching; PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, User stories

q: What does the "S" in INVEST stand for?
options: Specific
Small
Scheduled
Stable
explanation: INVEST: independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small, testable. A small story fits within one iteration.

q: What does a story point measure?
options: The number of hours a story will take
The business value of a user story, expressed in money
The relative effort needed to implement a user story
The number of people needed
explanation: A story point is a unit used to estimate the relative level of effort needed to implement a user story. It reflects relative effort or complexity, not absolute time.

q: Why do many agile teams estimate in story points instead of hours?
options: Teams are typically better at comparing work items than at predicting precise durations
Hours cannot be recorded in agile tools
Story points are required by law
Story points make it easy to compare teams
explanation: Story points rest on the understanding that teams are better at comparing items than at predicting exact durations. Estimating hours takes longer and is less reliable in dynamic environments.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Agile release planning

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Agile release planning

q: In planning poker, team members choose their estimate privately and then:
options: The product owner picks the final number
The lowest number is always used
The scrum master averages the numbers in secret and announces the result
All cards are revealed at the same time, and differences are discussed
explanation: Each team member privately selects a card, and when everyone is ready all cards are revealed together. This prevents the first number mentioned from anchoring the others.

q: What is velocity?
options: The speed at which the product owner writes stories
The rate at which the team produces, validates and accepts deliverables in a set interval
The number of hours worked per day
The number of defects found per iteration
explanation: Velocity is a measure of a team's productivity rate at which deliverables are produced, validated and accepted within a predefined interval.

q: A release has 150 story points of work remaining. The team's average velocity is 25 points per iteration. How many iterations are needed?
explanation: Iterations needed = remaining points ÷ velocity = 150 ÷ 25 = 6.

q: Team A has a velocity of 30 and Team B has a velocity of 50. What can be concluded?
options: Nothing about their relative productivity, because story points are specific to each team
Team B is more productive
Team A needs more people
Team B's stories are easier
explanation: Relative estimates are specific to the team doing the estimating, so they cannot be compared with other teams' numbers.

q: At the end of an iteration, one 8-point story is 90% complete. How many of its points count toward velocity?
explanation: Velocity counts deliverables that are produced, validated and accepted. An unfinished story earns nothing until it meets the definition of done.

q: What does agile release planning provide?
options: A task list for tomorrow
A high-level timeline of the release, typically 3 to 6 months, based on the product roadmap and vision
The detailed design of each feature
The final project budget
explanation: Agile release planning gives a high-level summary timeline of the release schedule, typically 3 to 6 months, and determines the number of iterations in the release.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Agile release planning

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Agile release planning

q: Which sequence correctly goes from the broadest plan to the most detailed?
options: Iteration plan, release plan, roadmap, vision
Release plan, vision, iteration plan, roadmap
Vision, roadmap, release plan, iteration plan
Roadmap, vision, iteration plan, release plan
explanation: The product vision drives the roadmap, the roadmap drives release planning, and release planning drives iteration planning.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Agile release planning

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Agile release planning

q: A backlog item is too large to complete in one iteration and spans many related stories. What is it usually called?
options: An epic
A task
A spike
A timebox
explanation: An epic is a large body of work that is broken down into features and user stories small enough to fit in an iteration.
ref: PMI Guide to Business Analysis, 4.6.2.5; PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Backlog

q: The team cannot estimate a story because it does not know whether a third-party interface supports a needed function. What should it do?
options: Guess a large number to be safe, and start building the feature anyway
Remove the story from the backlog
Ask the product owner to estimate it
Run a spike: a timeboxed piece of research to answer the question
explanation: A spike is a timeboxed user story or task created to research a question or resolve a problem.

q: What is a timebox?
options: A tool for recording hours worked
A short, fixed period of time in which work is to be completed
A deadline that can be extended whenever the work is not finished
A list of tasks
explanation: A timebox is a short, fixed period of time in which work is to be completed. When it ends, unfinished work returns to the backlog.

q: What is the definition of ready?
options: A checklist showing that a finished deliverable meets all criteria and is ready for customers
The date the team is available
A checklist showing a user story has all the information the team needs to begin work on it
The product owner's approval of a release
explanation: The definition of ready is a checklist for a user-centric requirement that has all the information the team needs to begin working on it. The definition of done covers completion.
ref: Agile Practice Guide, Glossary (definition of ready)

links.label: Agile Practice Guide, Glossary (definition of ready)

q: Who should estimate the size of user stories?
options: The team that will do the work
The product owner alone
The project sponsor
An external estimating department
explanation: Relative estimating is done by the team doing the work, using what the group knows. The product owner explains the story but does not estimate it.

q: During iteration planning, who decides how many stories the team will commit to?
options: The product owner, based on priority
The scrum master
The customer
The team, based on its capacity
explanation: Teams consider their capacity and story size so they do not commit to more than they can complete in one iteration.

q: Two team members will be on holiday during the next iteration. What should the team do in iteration planning?
options: Commit to the same amount of work as in any normal iteration
Plan only the amount of work that fits its reduced capacity
Cancel the iteration
Extend the iteration by a week
explanation: When people are unavailable the team cannot finish the same amount as before. With reduced capacity, a team plans only for work that meets that capacity.

q: What is backlog refinement?
options: Deleting the backlog at the end of the project
A meeting to demonstrate finished work
The progressive elaboration and reprioritization of backlog content to identify work for upcoming iterations
Assigning tasks to individuals
explanation: Backlog refinement means constantly reviewing, revising, ranking and editing the backlog so that the items for upcoming iterations are ready.

q: A story is estimated at 40 points, far larger than any other on the team's scale. What does this suggest?
options: The story should be split into smaller stories
The team should work overtime
The story should be done first
The scale should be changed from points to ideal hours
explanation: A very large estimate signals that the item is too big and too uncertain. Stories should be small enough to complete within an iteration, so it is split.
ref: PMI Guide to Business Analysis, 7.5.2.1; Agile Practice Guide, 5.2.2

q: A team moves a predictive project to an adaptive approach. What does a WBS work package usually become?
options: A single fixed milestone
A phase gate review
A schedule baseline
One or more user stories
explanation: In the usual mapping, major deliverables become epics or features and work packages become user stories, rewritten from the user's point of view and sliced to fit one iteration.

q: Which is a disadvantage of working in fixed-length iterations?
options: Feedback arrives every few weeks
Urgent work arriving mid-iteration disturbs the plan
Progress is measured in finished work
Risk is exposed early in the work
explanation: Iterations give rhythm, frequent feedback and early exposure of risk. Their cost is that stories must fit the timebox and unplanned urgent work disturbs the iteration; flow-based agile suits such work better.
